019530a6-cc5d-510e-8a02-0122394f5817.name: Revolver
019530a6-cc5d-510e-8a02-0122394f5817.description: The Lebel Revolver was the standard issue sidearm in the French military during the First World War, produced in Saint Etienne and used by the French army between 1892 and before 1924. The 1892 Model is a double/single action, six round cylinder revolver that fires 8-millimetre rounds. It was issued to officers in the French Army, Navy, and National Gendarmerie, amongst others. It is commonly called the Lebel Revolver after the gun designer Colonel Nicolas Lebel. For loading and releasing the empty cases, the chambers are accessed through swinging the cylinder to the right. Originally chambered for an 8mm gunpowder cartridge round, later models issued during World War I and thereafter fired the same 8mm cartridge loaded with smokeless powder. Serial number 21093.

0c19f7d6-2610-589f-a3df-5820477d393a.name: Captured arms (with accessories) from the occupation-campaign in Bosnia-Herzegovina 1878
0c19f7d6-2610-589f-a3df-5820477d393a.short_description: The 1878 Treaty of Berlin put the two Ottoman provinces of Bosnia and Herzegovina under the administration of the Austro-Hungarian Empire. Between the 20th of July and the 29th of October 1878, the Austro-Hungarian Empire led a military campaign in those two provinces in order to establish its administration. During this armed conflict, several objects were taken, like a 16mm flintlock pistol with an Oriental-style snaphaunce lock (miquelet lock) entirely wrought from iron and richly decorated, showing as high a quality of craftsmanship as the accompanying gunpowder pourers, ramrods and bullet pouches.

0e006c19-7de8-5aa1-b346-0a40a7dbcbd8.short_description: This bow quiver was in the collection of Archduke Ferdinand II of Tyrol (AD 1529–95) at Ambras Castle near Innsbruck. 0f137923-bf0e-59e9-aa6b-2af58599a73c.name: Flint lock pistol
0f137923-bf0e-59e9-aa6b-2af58599a73c.short_description: Following the fall of Seringapatam in 1799 AD, this gun was handed over to Lord Cornwallis (1738–1805 AD), a Governor General and Commander-in-Chief of British army during the third Anglo-Mysorean war (1789–1792 AD) as a trophy. The gun is rich with tiger motifs with complete form of tiger figure on the butt and stylised *bubri* on the barrel as well as inscriptions on different parts of the gun. Images of tigers mauling European soldier on the side plate of the gun represents Tipu’s propaganda in degrading the British East India Company. The gun possessed advanced technology of its time where shooter could fire twice continuously with only a single load.

117e4311-5f29-5b99-9692-18b2ed19cd70.short_description: The handle of this sabre is set with ivory, the crossguard with large sapphires and emeralds; the blade is decorated with gilt engraved etchings that contain the year AD 1813 and the name of Fath Ali (AD 1797–1834), the then reigning Shah. 156506f6-1fb1-58ab-8228-704b9a0cd0f9.short_description: This sword was likely made for the Ottoman Sultan Süleyman the Magnificent (r. 1520–66). Its blade is chiselled in relief with Qur’anic verses, with the surrounding areas inlaid in gold. Its guard is chiselled with gold-damascened flowers and was formerly inlaid with rubies. The grip, covered with dyed green fishskin (shagreen), is a later replacement.

1a6fd108-7bb7-5e52-b70a-6d8c81c37f18.name: Battle-shield with coat of arms inspired by Oriental motifs
1a6fd108-7bb7-5e52-b70a-6d8c81c37f18.description: Some people like to claim that everything used to be better in the old days. Indeed, the oldest extant battle-shield, too, once shone in bright colours. Analysis has shown that, 800 years ago, the greyish green used to be a vibrant blue. The lion, too, wasn’t always as lacklustre as it is now; it used to stand out in shiny silver leaf. The shield belonged to the noble von Brienz family, which used to hold feudal rights in today’s Canton of Uri, on the road to the Gotthard pass. When its owner, the knight Arnold von Brienz, died in 1225, his battle-shield was placed above his tomb in commemoration of his deeds. This is how it survived the ages. The shield’s many notches, holes and nicks remind us of the brutal reality of medieval battles.

1d0bb991-65bb-5ca4-a706-534f9745fd08.name: *Saif* (Straight, double-edged sword)
1d0bb991-65bb-5ca4-a706-534f9745fd08.short_description: Until recently it was a rare occurrence for Omani artisans, poets, authors and others to sign their work. This custom of anonymity reflects the central belief of Ibadhi Muslims that work is done for the glory of God, not for the glory of self. Today, this custom of humility before God persists, with work being signed for reasons of practicality, not self-aggrandisement. Signatures are typically modest in terms of scale, placement and style of execution. This blade is a rare example, stamped on one side indicating it as "The work of Ali bin Rah'meen". It is common now for artisans to sign their work with the name of the town or *souq* (local market) where their workshop is located in lieu of a personal signature.

1e88ab3a-3f62-5a22-b9a2-264a8573788d.name: Two pistols
1e88ab3a-3f62-5a22-b9a2-264a8573788d.short_description: These Turkish flintlock pistols were used by the Ottoman soldiers in Lebanon in the 19th century to quash resistance movements. As the Lebanese resistance had no weapons of their own, the fighters frequently ambushed Ottoman soldiers and took their weapons. These pistols are an example of such weaponry, which was taken by the resistance and used against the Ottomans. They were commonly known as "knee pistols", as they were fired from horseback by placing the butt of the pistol against the rider's knee. Both have a typical blunderbuss style stock with a beautifully shaped butt stock, a wooden forend and a round barrel. They are made of wood and cast steel.

1eb2a94c-9bbe-50cd-9506-87b470659f68.name: Moorish shield (*adarga*)
1eb2a94c-9bbe-50cd-9506-87b470659f68.short_description: The shape of this shield is derived from North African and Moorish models. The name of this kidney-shaped shield also informed the name of an oval shield popular in the Occident, the *Tartsche*. The *adarga* is covered with colourful silk embroidery, suggesting a high-ranking owner. The shield, now in Vienna, probably entered the Habsburg collections when Juana I of Castile (AD 1479–1555) married Philip I (Philip the Handsome) (AD 1478–1506). In the late 16th century the shield was in the collection of Archduke Ferdinand II (AD 1529–95) at Ambras Castle near Innsbruck.

34093957-9215-5f74-8896-55c092200e01.name: Artillery piece – Half-cannon – Muzzleloader
34093957-9215-5f74-8896-55c092200e01.description:
Although the military armaments industry of India and China flourished more than it did in Europe in the early 15th century, developments in Europe took advantage later in the century – the Portuguese learning armament techniques. During the 16th and 17th centuries with their arrival in China, the Portuguese were able to profit from their ability to help the warring factions in the Chinese Empire. In Japan, the Shogun authorities learned about guns from the Portuguese in the 16th century.  
This half-canon dates to the 17th-century. Cast in bronze, it has a caliber of 13.8 cm and a length of 3.62 m; it weighs over 3026 kg. It uses iron canon balls of 8.2 kg.  
The object displays the coat of arms of the city of Macao in China, below which is a rampant lion with a Marquis' crown. Engraved in a frame is the following inscription: “ANT. TELES DE MENEZES Govºr DA INDIA A MANDOU FAZER NO ANO DE 1640” (“ANTONIO TELES DE MENEZES GOVERNOR OF INDIA ORDERED IT TO BE MADE IN 1640”).  
Holding in its breech the name of the Caster “M\[anu\]el TAVARES BOCARRO”, as a personal touch, the cascable ending is in the shape of a lotus flower. Manuel Tavares Bocarro, son of Pedro Dias Bocarro also a gun founder, was the leading officer of the gun foundry of cannons in the Chunambeiro, Macao, during the mid-17th century. The cannons he produced were famous worldwide; two of them are in the Tower of London.

3a110f14-cb1d-5cf4-bcbf-686eae047043.name: Horse bridle.
3a110f14-cb1d-5cf4-bcbf-686eae047043.description:
A part of a bridle or halter that would have been placed around a horse’s head; made of gold and enamel sections through which leather straps pass. These small oblong-shaped sections are decorated with gold filigree alternating with blue, red, white and green cloisonné enamel. The enamel compartments are filled with arabesques in opaque red and white against a background of translucent green and blue. The style and decorative techniques belong to a long tradition in Islamic Spain. However, the design of this bridle relates to Nasrid architecture, in particular certain stucco panels in the Alhambra Palace in Granada. Therefore this piece was certainly made in Granada but not necessarily for a Muslim patron.  
The decoration on this bridle can be connected to that seen on a hilt and scabbard (in the Museo del Ejercito), and a scabbard and mounts of a dagger (in the Real Armería). Previously in the collection of the Vieana Family, it has been suggested that after the battle of Lucana in AH 887/ AD 1483, one of the ancestors of this family took these pieces of armoury, which had belonged to Abu Abd Allah Muhammad XI (or Boabdil) the last sultan of the Nasrid dynasty of Granada (r. AH 886–96 / AD 1482–92).
3a110f14-cb1d-5cf4-bcbf-686eae047043.short_description: It is uncertain exactly where and when this luxury horse bridle was made. Gold and enamel decoration belonged to a long tradition known in many parts of Islamic Spain, however, it was probably made for the Nasrid court as the design recalls certain stucco panels in the Alhambra Palace in Granada.
3a110f14-cb1d-5cf4-bcbf-686eae047043.dates: Hegira late 9th–early 10th century / AD late 15th–early 16th century.
3a110f14-cb1d-5cf4-bcbf-686eae047043.method_for_datation:
This bridle is close in design to a group of objects associated with Abu Abd Allah Muhammad XI (or Boabdil), the last sultan of the Nasrid dynasty of Granada (r. 886–96 / 1482–92).  
Although it is not certain that it was made for this ruler, the technique and design fit with other gold and enamel work produced in the late 9th / 15th century.

3d5efcb2-fd89-51e3-ac74-47777b9edbb6.name: Saber (*shamshir*)
3d5efcb2-fd89-51e3-ac74-47777b9edbb6.short_description:
Attributed to Imam Saif bin Sultan al-Yarubi I (*Qaid al-Ard’*)  
*Collections of Sultan Qaboos bin Said bin Taimur*  
  
The blade of this saber is by Asadallah of Isfahan, one of the most celebrated swordsmiths of Islamic civilisation in the Hegira 11th century / AD 17th century. It is made from Damascus steel and patterned with the most complex design, known as the “forty steps”. The swordsmith’s signature appears in the middle gold cartouche of the blade reading “the work of Asadallah 186”, and “property of Sheikh Saif” in the lower cartouche, as well as the inscription “Shah Abas year 5”.  
  
The blade’s inscription proves that the sabre was not taken as loot. Rather, the maker had been commissioned directly. The design and inscriptions make it likely that it was made for presentation to Saif, perhaps by the Safavid Court of Persia, who, in Hegira 1086 / AD 1675, saw him as a future leader of Oman.

40b94627-118d-5dff-a831-ecd2614c6078.name: Turban Helmet
40b94627-118d-5dff-a831-ecd2614c6078.short_description: Helmets of this type are traditionally referred to as turban helmets because of their bulbous shape. The wide bowl of the helmet was forged from a single plate of steel tapering to a separately attached finial at the top. The bowl preserves several of the pierced lugs for the attachment of mail, which protected the neck. Just above the fitted opening for the eyes is a remnant of the sliding *nasil* bar and its bracket, now missing. Above and below the wide band of fluted groves at the center of the bowl are silver inlaid inscription bands in *naskh* on a scrolling ground; the text reads in part: Everlasting glory and prosperity to the…sultan. Incised above the left eye cup is the mark or *tamğa* of the Ottoman arsenal, suggesting that the helmet was taken to Turkey as booty.

40b94627-118d-5dff-a831-ecd2614c6078.method_for_datation: Such helmets are usually attributed to lands controlled by the Aq Quyunlu dynasty. This helmet is especially close to an example in the Metropolitan Museum (04.3.211), likewise incised with the mark of the Ottoman arsenal and inscribed perhaps with the name of the Aq Quyunlu Sultan Yaqub (Hegira 883-896 / AD 1478-1490) and can thereby be similarly dated.
40b94627-118d-5dff-a831-ecd2614c6078.method_for_provenance: Helmets of this type are generally associated with the Aq Quyunlu dynasty (Hegira 780-914/1378-1508 AD), which ruled northwestern Iran and eastern Anatolia.

42a95db0-705d-5ebb-926f-d8bab4c95c82.name: Sword.
42a95db0-705d-5ebb-926f-d8bab4c95c82.description:
A sword composed of a double-edged curved blade, a crosspiece and a hilt. The crosspiece assumes the form of a cross: the short side is adhered to the hilt and blade, while the long side projects from the blade and runs perpendicular to it, ending in two oval ornamented units. The blade is decorated with gilt inscriptions, bearing the name of the Mamluk Sultan al-Adil Tumanbay, who ruled for several months only and was deposed in the month of Ramadan in AH 907 (1501). The inscription reads: 'The sultan, al-Malik al-Adil Abu al-Nasr Tumanbay, Sultan of Islam and the Muslims, Father of the Poor and Miserable, Destroyer of Infidels and Idolators, Reviver of Justice to all. May God grant him a lasting reign and may his triumph be glorious'.  
In general, swords from the Mamluk Period were embellished with gilt inscriptions that included the name of the sultan and their title; occasionally verses from the Qur'an were also engraved on them. The office of the *silahdar* (weapon bearer) was one of the highest positions in the Mamluk state, thus *amirs* who ascended to this position often had the form of the sword represented in their blazons.  
Islamic swords were forged from Syrian steel, which was considered one of the best available. Swords were crafted in two parts: a pliable iron foil and a rigid one, they were then hammered together.
42a95db0-705d-5ebb-926f-d8bab4c95c82.short_description: One of the terrifying Mamluk weapons, the sword was used in war, for hunting and on courtly occasions. Swords were usually decorated with gilt inscriptions praising their owners, like this double-edged sword bearing the name of Sultan al-Adil al-Nasr Tumanbay.
42a95db0-705d-5ebb-926f-d8bab4c95c82.initial_owner: Al-Adil Sayf al-Din Tumanbay (reigned for a few months only, deposed Ramadan AH 907 (1501)).
42a95db0-705d-5ebb-926f-d8bab4c95c82.method_for_datation: The sword is dated based on the inscription carved on the blade: 907 (1501).
42a95db0-705d-5ebb-926f-d8bab4c95c82.method_for_provenance: It is likely that the sword was made in Egypt, particularly as it carries the name of Sultan Tumanbay, the ruler of Egypt at the time.
42a95db0-705d-5ebb-926f-d8bab4c95c82.provenance: It is likely that this piece was forged in Cairo.
42a95db0-705d-5ebb-926f-d8bab4c95c82.obtention: This piece was bought in 1919 from an antiquities dealer, Janon.

45ccc1b2-62ae-540c-ba7c-d71565ea58c3.name: Palestine Gendarmerie badge
45ccc1b2-62ae-540c-ba7c-d71565ea58c3.description: The Palestine Gendarmerie, established on 1 July 1921, consisted of Arabs and Jews under British officers. It consisted of cavalry, camelry and infantry units. Enlistment of recruits was regulated so as to maintain a certain proportion amongst the various sects and religious creeds, which comprised Arabs, Jews, Circassians and Druse. In 1922, the strength of the Palestine Gendarmerie was as follows: 234 Arabs, 157 Jews, 72 Circassians and 27 Druses, of whom 250 were mounted on horses and 50 on camels, the remainder consisting of infantry. The badge was usually seen worn on black kalpak hats. It consists of the British imperial crown leaned on the letters PG, the abbreviation of Palestine Gendarmerie written in capital French script. Two crossed flags in the middle of the letters PG, based on a band that displays the full name of the PALESTINE GENDARMERIE and below the date 1921 written on a small band. The flag in the right side is broken.

53b64031-daec-570d-8bd3-6cd325cad7a9.name: Dagger (Tams Type)
53b64031-daec-570d-8bd3-6cd325cad7a9.short_description: This dagger provides an excellent example of the Arabesque in Islamic design. The term, "Arabesque", can be defined in two ways; as a specific decorative element consisting of a continuous branching stem with split palmate leaves, or in a larger sense, used to refer to an entire range of designs based on stylised floral, foliar and animal motifs. The aesthetics of the Arabesque are derived from the imposition of order on the natural world. Arabesque patterns are used extensively in traditional Omani woodwork, plasterwork and metalwork as a means of covering entire surfaces or precise areas within a defined geometric framework.

58ffe3b7-a7c4-59ea-a3f7-15adee4841cf.name: Sword that belonged to Carol of Hohenzollern
58ffe3b7-a7c4-59ea-a3f7-15adee4841cf.short_description: In April 1866, Carol of Hohenzollern was elected by plebiscite ruler of the United Principalities of Moldavia and Wallachia. However, according to the Paris Convention of 1858, an act signed by the Ottoman Empire, Russia, Austria, Prussia, France, Great Britain and Sardinia, which established the internal organization of the Principalities, they were supposed to each have their own local prince. So, Carol’s election had to be recognized by the Sublime Porte, the sovereign power, and by the other Great Powers. Following negotiations held at Istanbul, in October sultan Abdul Aziz agreed to give his consent. Carol then travelled to Istanbul, where he was invested as ruler of the Principalities and was given by the sultan five Arabian horses and a sword decorated with 1140 brilliants and 46 diamonds.

59c2a789-38b6-526c-8c2e-10450f77128f.name: Long Moorish musket

The Moorish musket, a long firearm that could be shot with a single arm while riding the horse, was described by Salvador as “one of the most ancient and authentic", a truly beauty with damascene work, romantically infused with the testimony of the war.

5b111959-0e06-5d73-9d98-5177f4d07663.short_description: In the AD 1559 inventory of the collection of Archduke Ferdinand II of Tyrol (AD 1529–95) this helmet and cuirassier armour were wrongly attributed to "N. König zu Cuba in India“ (a king of Cuba in India). In AD 1788 the shield was correctly added and the ensemble, for no apparent reason, identified as belonging to the North African maritime hero, Dragut Reis, King of Kairun (died AD 1565). Modern attribution to a Mamluk prince is based on the artefact's similarity to the *morion* (open helmet) of Khairbak, the Mamluk governor of Aleppo (Istanbul, Topkapı Sarayı Museum) who handed over Syria to the Ottoman Sultan Selim I in AD 1517. It is the most sumptuous example of this type of Oriental armour.

6d67dd68-9a25-5aff-9ff7-90c6c6b016bb.name: Dagger handle.
6d67dd68-9a25-5aff-9ff7-90c6c6b016bb.description: A dagger handle made of ivory, carved with arabesque patterns and two narrow horizontal bands with circular motifs. In contrast to the popularity of ivory carving in other periods of Islamic art, such as under the Umayyads of Spain, Ottoman works in carved ivory are relatively rare. Those that were made, however, are exquisite; they include hand-mirror backings, belt segments, and dagger handles like this one. The surface is carved with arabesque motifs which strongly recall the so-called 'Baba Naqqash' style, a distinctive Ottoman idiom that employs traditional Islamic arabesques combined with Chinese elements, and one which remained fashionable in other media long after it had gone out of style in ceramics. An ivory dagger handle much like this one is owned by the British Museum (inv. no. OA 409), while a dagger made in AH 949 / AD 1543 in Ottoman-ruled Hungary has a gilt-silver handle with similar decoration (National Museum of Hungary, 55.3237). 6f3c1d83-c1d2-5207-a72e-e6b0bd916f8d.short_description: The Ottoman sword is made by one of the master sword smiths of the late 18th and early 19th century, Ahmad al-Khurasani. All share similar elements and standard decorations of typical Ottoman swords produced in the 18th and 19th centuries. This style highlights the curved blade with chiselled and gilded foliage on a recess and *kufic* inscription arranged along the blade. The hilt takes the shape of a pistol grip made of horn and the wooden scabbard mounted with gilded sheets. The blade has been inscribed with Qur’anic verses and signed with the maker’s name in square *kufic* panel.

7ec5b54e-b5f6-55dc-bba6-dbab52faa88a.name: Yataghan from the court of Süleyman the Magnificent (r. 1520–66)

The gold incrustation on the blade depicts a combat between a dragon and a phoenix against a background of foliate scrolls. These figures, like the gold-inlaid cloud bands and foliate scrolls on the ivory grips, are Chinese in inspiration, and were probably introduced into Ottoman art through contacts with Persia.

87839162-d295-566b-8702-37a9e59ccbec.name: Cap Helmet (*kulah khud*) with Design of Interlaced Vines, Arabic Inscriptions, and Mail Neck Curtain
87839162-d295-566b-8702-37a9e59ccbec.short_description:
A hemispherical cap helmet (*kulah khud*) with a four-sided spike attached to the top. Approximately a quarter of the way down the spike from its tip the sides are flat, then they become deeply fluted, creating four sharp ridges. Each flute is decorated with diamond-shapes of varying sizes in gold overlay. The spike then joins a gold leafed ball atop a conical foot, sides decorated in vegetal and geometric designs in gold.  
The majority of the helmet is decorated in a regular, intertwined pattern of arabesques, and there is a band around the bottom with a much more dense pattern of geometric and vegetal decoration, interspersed with Arabic inscriptions. Attached at the front, center of the helmet is a vertical, squared rod that follows the curve of the helmet. It is attached by a short, horizontal clamp attached to the helmet with two rivets, and decorated with gold overlay. The ends of the vertical bar flatten into leaves decorated in gold. A short distance, both to the left and right of the vertical bar, is a short, vertical, hollow rod that flattens into a leaf at its bottom end, also riveted to the helmet.  
The bottom lip of the helmet is perforated around the circumference with small circular holes for the attachment of thin wire jump rings. To these rings is attached a network of circular links, forming an aventail or mail neck curtain that hangs short across the front of the helmet, then longer around the remainder, coming to six triangular points.  
The helmet is in good condition, with the exception of a number of deep nicks and abrasions around the top of the spike, and the chain mail is missing some areas at the back of the helmet.

969f28d7-18db-53c5-8afc-a2bab8697217.name: Shirt of Mail and Plate

9759fb2e-169a-5a39-8d80-11289577854b.name: Al-Haswa Dagger (*khanjar*)
9759fb2e-169a-5a39-8d80-11289577854b.short_description:
Attributed to Imam Saif bin Sultan al-Yarubi I (*Qaid al-Ard’*)  
Collections of Sultan Qaboos bin Said bin Taimur  
  
Saif bin Sultan I was the fourth of the al-Ya’aruba dynasty Imams of Oman (ruled Hegira 1104–23 / AD 1692–1711). He made the ar-Rustaq Fort his residence, adding the *Burj al-Riah,* “the wind tower”.  
  
The Omani navy reached a great degree of development during the Imam’s reign, where his foreign policy was based on renewing the struggle against the Portuguese on the Persian, Indian and East African coasts. In Hegira 1110 / AD 1696, the Omani naval fleet attacked Mombasa, besieging the Portuguese who had taken refuge in Fort Jesus. The Siege of Fort Jesus (also known as the Battle of Mombasa), ended after 33 months when the remaining survivors surrendered. Soon after the Omanis took Pemba, Kilwa and Zanzibar, becoming the dominant power on the coast.  
  
At home, Imam Saif bin Sultan invested in agrarian reform, building new *aflaj* water management systems and maintaining old systems; expanding the plantation of crops such as wheat, barley and sugar cane; planting date palm and fruit trees; introducing new varieties of plants such as turmeric, saffron and coffee; and establishing beekeeping.  
  
Saif bin Sultan earned the title Qaid al-Ard’ meaning "the Earth's bond" or "the chain of the Earth" for the benefits he brought to the people of Oman.

99c365eb-e061-5123-97ee-c6128fee870f.name: Arab / Bedouin Gun
99c365eb-e061-5123-97ee-c6128fee870f.short_description: This matchlock musket, locally made based on a European prototype, is known as 'Abu Futtila'. It is an  example of the type of weapon used from the early 18th century until as late as the early 20th century in the Arabian Peninsula. The type was typically simply stocked, but generally as with this example, fitted with an extremely high quality barrel.  The tang is stamped with a maker's mark. This gun is a good example as it retains what is possibly its original match consisting of twisted fibre cord bound with cotton and two large copper alloy tubular fittings,  probably to hold lighted sections of the match. The gun is muzzle loaded and has a  .50 calibre smoothbore barrel with a single shot firing capacity. The musket shows fine fluting and has a chiseled barrel with geometric designs and silver inlay, as well as a copper alloy mounted forward grip. The copper taper holders under the wick do not appear to be original, but this gun still has its primer pan protector.Weapons were among the most coveted and desirable, if often illicit commodities in the Arab Gulf. European weapons were mainly imported through Muscat and Bushire on the Persian coast of the Gulf, with many than copied locally.

a34c1a9f-ced6-5d46-9b24-f76e88d32863.name: Sword.
a34c1a9f-ced6-5d46-9b24-f76e88d32863.description:
This sword, produced in the Mongol style, consists of four parts: the blade, hilt, cross-guard and scabbard. This style of weaponry, which filtered through to Persia, was known by the name of *al-Shamshir.*  
The blade is narrow and tapers at the head. It is attached at the top by a wooden hilt in the middle of which is a notch 1.5 cm wide. Inserted in the blade is a copper band decorated with gold lines. A cross-guard separates the blade from the hilt assuming a cruciform shape, and the long side of which is perpendicular to the hilt and the sword blade, its two sides ending in two ornamental globules. There is an inscription on each side of the cross-guard.  
The blade also bears decorative engraved inscriptions such as Qur'anic verses, popular sayings and poetry stanzas. One of the two edges of the sword bears illuminated inscriptions with an illuminated frame. One of them reads: “There is no hero like 'Ali and no sword like Zulfikar”. And another reads: “Oh Judge of Necessities”. Written on the blade at the hilt is the following text: “Victory is from God and Conquest is near, year AH 785 \[AD 1383\]”. There are two non-illuminated inscriptions engraved on the blade within a cartouche. The first reads: “The work of As'ad Allah”. And the second: “‘Abbas bi Nadir Shah”. In the middle of the blade is an inscription that extends approximately 43 cm. It consists of what is probably popular poetry and begins with the verse: “Unsheath the sword of destruction from its scabbard of support and cleave with it, the preponderance of envy and aggression”.  
The scabbard is made of wood, copper-plated at the top to about 18.5 cm. There are three engraved inscriptions written in *thuluth* script on the copper section. The inscriptions are contained within a linear frame that is surrounded by depictions of flowers and vegetal stems. The copper section is adjacent to two bands each of which is 7 cm wide. A 27.5 cm-long copper section at the end of the scabbard holds five inscriptions; its decoration is similar to that on the copper hilt. In the area between the two copper sections, the scabbard is covered with a piece of carpet-like fabric 47 cm long, woven in red, brown and gold. The inscriptions on the scabbard include popular sayings and poetry in praise of the sword and supplications to God for victory.
a34c1a9f-ced6-5d46-9b24-f76e88d32863.short_description: This sword consists of the scabbard, blade, hilt and cross-guard. It is in the Mongol style, which was taken to Persia. It has a narrow blade and the cross guard has a cruciform shape.  The sword is filled with inscriptions and vegetal decoration. The date engraved on it does not concur with the lifespan of its maker, As'ad Allah.
a34c1a9f-ced6-5d46-9b24-f76e88d32863.holder: Islamic Museum, al-Aqsa Mosque / al-Haram al-Sharif.
a34c1a9f-ced6-5d46-9b24-f76e88d32863.dimensions: Entire length 107 cm, length (of blade) 90 cm, width (of blade) 3.3 cm, length (of Scabbard) 93 cm.
a34c1a9f-ced6-5d46-9b24-f76e88d32863.method_for_datation: This sword has an inscribed date on it, but like tens of other swords it poses a historical puzzle. The date of production engraved on it does not agree with the life-span of the original owner, Shah ‘Abbas I. In addition, it does not concur with the life-span of its craftsman, As'ad Allah, who was a renowned sword-maker and a contemporary of Shah ‘Abbas. It is worth noting that there are about 300 swords distributed in museums worldwide that are associated with As'ad Allah and bear his name. The oldest of them is the sword exhibited here, which dates to 785 / 1383; the most recent dates to 1223/ 1808. Thus, the association of the swords to this skilled craftsman continued for more than four centuries.
a34c1a9f-ced6-5d46-9b24-f76e88d32863.method_for_provenance: Iran has been narrowed down as the place of manufacture of this sword because the craftsman associated with it and original owner have links with Iran.

a5b2fd9b-e8df-5b2a-b618-52f1601e4e7a.name: Powder container.
a5b2fd9b-e8df-5b2a-b618-52f1601e4e7a.description:
This very curved horn-shaped container is made of wood covered with red velvet. It was fitted with two rings that enabled it to be attached to a rider's neck or waist with a strap. The mouth, tip and centre are decorated with cylindrical and conical plaques in gilded, engraved silver openwork. Whether embroidered with gold thread on the velvet covering or engraved and rendered in openwork on the silver plaques, the decoration consists mainly of plant motifs: stems, foliage, palms and fleurons borrowed from the traditional artistic repertoire of Morocco and Andalusia. A single geometric element, an eight-pointed star that marks the centre of the central metal plaque, stands alone among the plant decoration.  
This type of container, whose curving shape is reminiscent of the Yemen *jambiya* dagger, contained the powder used to load the rifles used in the *fantasia* and was part of the equipment carried by the horsemen of the north of Morocco who took part in games on richly harnessed steeds.

They were carried by the horsemen of Northern Morocco who participated in such games on sumptuously harnessed horses.

a9281dfb-f5ce-5f06-9747-94bf00a2f99e.name: Shield
a9281dfb-f5ce-5f06-9747-94bf00a2f99e.short_description: These shields were used by the Ottoman soldiers in Lebanon in the 19th century to quash resistance movements. As the Lebanese resistance had no weapons of their own, the fighters frequently ambushed Ottoman soldiers and took their weapons. This shield is an example of such weaponry, which was taken by the resistance and used against the Ottomans. It was used mainly by foot soldiers, and was hand-held with straps going around the wearer's arm. Although ineffective against newer weaponry such as guns, the shield was used by soldiers to deflect arrows or swords. It is made of cast steel, with no decorative elements of notes. It features four bosses and reverse arm fixings.

aa69e40a-8b6f-5533-b199-6d9e6bc16fba.name: *Ghazal* (Knife)
aa69e40a-8b6f-5533-b199-6d9e6bc16fba.short_description: The highest quality of these pocket knives have a blade made of steel and handle made of the core of a ghazal’s horns. The sheath is usually made of wood and decorated with silver plated leather. Arabesque patterns are used extensively in traditional Omani woodwork, plasterwork and metalwork as a means of covering entire surfaces or precise areas within a defined geometric framework. The symmetry of this design can be noted in this excellent example, a *ghazal* (knife) from the mid-20th century. The term, "Arabesque", can be defined in two ways within the context of Islamic design; as a specific decorative element consisting of a continuous branching stem with split palmate leaves, or in a larger sense, referring to an entire range of designs based on stylised floral, foliar and animal motifs. The aesthetics of the Arabesque are derived from the imposition of order on the natural world.
aa69e40a-8b6f-5533-b199-6d9e6bc16fba.dates: Mid 14th century AH / Mid 20th century AD

The inscription surrounds the blade opening. Lion heads adorn the quillions (the horizontal element of the handle which protects the hand). The handle and blade openings are surrounded by finely worked gold twisted rope rings. The handle socket is octagonal, its panels alternating between sides of overall-engraved scrollwork, with single delicate arabesque designs in the center. The cross-section of the handle socket is octagonal.

c57df15d-93f3-5f9e-bece-295781bfd341.name: British incendiary bomb from World War II
c57df15d-93f3-5f9e-bece-295781bfd341.description: Composed of a steel shell and a detonator, this bomb weighs around 6.2 kg and is 82.5 cm long. It is connected to a cotton parachute measuring 35cm in diameter. When the parachute opened, the bomb was armed; it was intended also to allow the bomb to strike the ground upright, point first – only in this way was it able to detonate. By the time of the armistice on 22 June 1940, Nazi Germany had occupied northern France and had effective control of the south of the country. Eight days later, a British bomber jettisoned this incendiary device at 0100 hours on 30 June 1940 above Altmatt in central Switzerland. Although the warring parties were prohibited from flying over neutral Switzerland, its airspace was regularly violated. It is not known why the bomb was jettisoned, but it certainly failed to detonate on impact. The Swiss Army impounded the unexploded bomb, and on 4th July 1940, the signals battalion produced a report that is restricted to a detailed technical description of its construction and workings. Made in Norwich and dropped over Switzerland one summer’s night, this World War II bomb was finally handed over to the Swiss National Museum in 1976.

ca942ff7-606f-5ad2-bbe5-0716cf554458.name: Prick spur.
ca942ff7-606f-5ad2-bbe5-0716cf554458.description: Originally one of a pair of prick spurs, this spur would have been fixed to footwear, to the sides of the ankle, with the prick pointing out at the back of the heel. A horse-rider (cavalryman, horse-archer, or knight) would use it to prick his horse when commanding it to move or run. The spur has straight sides with two holes at the end of each for the straps that tie around the ankles. These two straight sides meet in the middle to form an elliptical arch. Attached to the point where the two sides meet is a section that has a conical shaped tip (the prick). The spur's straight sides indicate that it could not have been made after the AH 6th century / AD 12th century, while the two strap-holes on the end of the sides of the spur show that this item was not likely to have been made before 1100.
ca942ff7-606f-5ad2-bbe5-0716cf554458.short_description: Every Crusader knight, cavalryman and horse-archer would have had a pair of prick spurs like these fixed onto the heel of their footwear. The European Crusader would use the prick to coax his horse into moving or picking up speed.

d5394661-4645-57e7-b329-fa21ef1c08fd.name: Scaled armours (cuirass), and swords.
d5394661-4645-57e7-b329-fa21ef1c08fd.description:
Two iron and ivory swords and two protective lamellar cuirasses or scaled armour, made out of overlapping metal rings. Usually worn over a thick linen or leather shirt, the cuirass protected the soldier from direct sword, arrow or dagger hits during battle. Sometimes it was hidden under a surcoat (burda).  
  
There were two main types of cuirasses: the first was wider and more constrictive, although more protective; while the second was a shorter, sleeveless cuirass that allowed more freedom of movement, but which offered less protection. Foot soldiers and archers were known to cut the sleeves off their cuirasses because of the weight and hindrance of movement.  
  
Protective armours have a long history and are therefore difficult to date. In the AH 6th–7th / AD 12th–13th century, the manufacture of scaled armours reached its peak, especially during the Crusader wars. Cuirasses like this one were made of copper, steal and Iron.  
  
The Arabs greatly valued the sword, giving it more than 100 different names. In the Middle Islamic period (AH 6th–10th / AD 12th–15th centuries) the manufacture of swords, shields and armour was active in Damascus, Cairo and Aleppo. Sometimes the name of the maker appears on the sword itself like 'Ali' who made the sword of the Mamluk Sultan Husam al-Din Lajin (r. AH 695–8 / AD 1296–9) and 'Hajji Yusuf' from Aleppo who made the sword of Sultan Qaytbay (r. AH 872–901 / AD 1468–96).
d5394661-4645-57e7-b329-fa21ef1c08fd.short_description: Two iron and ivory swords and two protective lamellar cuirasses, or scaled armour, made out of overlapping metal rings. dd44c4b3-03fc-5979-8e45-d6162ea57c5a.name: Sword.
dd44c4b3-03fc-5979-8e45-d6162ea57c5a.description: Although this sword was not found in Crusader lands, it is a typical example of a Crusader sword brought to the Holy Land and used by European warriors and knights. The sword has a double-edged slashing blade, which tapers off to a sharp point. It has a central, single channel (fuller) running along the blade on each side, the presence of which lightens the sword without affecting its strength thus making it more effective for cutting and hacking. The handle has a pommel (the knob at the top of the grip) in the shape of a chamfered wheel that is inlaid with brass in the form of a cross design on one side, and a design consisting of three half circles linked in the middle with three lines, on the other. This type of pommel came into use in about the AH 5th / AD 11th century, when sword blades increased in length too. Despite the disappointing number of artefacts that have survived from the Crusades, contemporary European manuscripts and their miniature paintings, together with monuments and their carvings, have depicted with impressive accuracy the types of arms and armour used during the Crusader period.

e3f7d3b9-509a-5b0d-8591-95270af03e15.name: Horse tack.
e3f7d3b9-509a-5b0d-8591-95270af03e15.description:
This full set of horse tack includes a saddle, cloth, bridle, collar, stirrups, saddlebags and girths. These elements, which used numerous different materials and trades in their manufacture, were the work of many craftsmen and women employed by the master saddler.  
The wooden tree (the frame of the saddle) is covered with a camel-skin shabraque (saddle-cloth). It differs from European saddles with its two very high arches. The saddle cloth, which was placed on top of the shabraque, brow band, visor, collar, girth and breast strap that kept the saddle on the horse's back, as well as the two saddlebags attached with a strap, were made of leather and black serge embroidered with gold thread. These items were further embellished with trim, thick braids and fringes in black and yellow silk. The breast strap is embellished with two large oval leather studs decorated with floral motifs in champlevé enamel. The iron stirrups are damascened in gold.  
The decoration on the saddle uses vegetal and plant motifs, foliage, palms and fleurons arranged within compartments framed by the foliage. Intertwined plant designs are used on the backs of the high arches of the saddle, as is the five-pointed star, which is stamped on the front of the saddlebags. The gold-thread decoration on the harness would have been designed by the saddlers and embroidered by women, who would also have woven the silk cords and braids at home.  
This type of sumptuous saddle would have adorned horses in the town and in the country during festival days and parades, in particular for the *fantasias* that took place on certain important religious or national occasions.
e3f7d3b9-509a-5b0d-8591-95270af03e15.short_description: This type of luxury harness and saddle was worn by horses on feast days and parades, in particular the *fantasia* tournaments that were held on certain important religious or national events. The saddle is different from European saddles as it has a tree with two high arches.
e3f7d3b9-509a-5b0d-8591-95270af03e15.method_for_datation: By the type of embroidery used.

ea93f27b-2ec2-5723-a1f1-65b29d221852.name: *Talahiq* (Gunpowder Horn)
ea93f27b-2ec2-5723-a1f1-65b29d221852.short_description:
Arabic is a poetic language with expressive power, and Omanis are known to be articulate and moving storytellers and poets. Arabic calligraphy, prized as a means of communication and adornment, gives form to literary expression within a visual context. The traditional art of verbal expression remains popular in Oman today, and master poets and storytellers are held in high esteem. Proverbs, whether recited or written, serve as a means of imparting wisdom and human truths based on common sense and often take the form of a metaphor or a poem. Sources of proverbs include the sayings of the Prophet Muhammed and other thinkers and theologians.  
  
This gunpowder horn, which comes from the period of Imam Said bin Ahmed al-Busai’idi (r. 1783-1810 AD), the 2nd ruler of the al-Busai’idi of Oman and the son of Imam Ahmed, founder of the al-Busai’idi Dynasty, was designed to fill the powder pan of a matchlock gun. The large decorative top was removable for filling the horn, and the gunpowder was released at the narrow end by operating the lever along the inner curve. The horn is made of silver, which has been layered with gold, and it is decorated with stamped and chased work suggesting that it belonged to a prominent person. An extract of a poem by al-Mutannabi, a renowned 10th century AD poet, is inscribed on the side of the horn:  
  
'If death is inevitable ... Then it is shameful to die a coward.'

ed60638d-d98c-52c9-b631-d363eb97fb51.name: *Jineta* Sword.
ed60638d-d98c-52c9-b631-d363eb97fb51.description:
Sword consisting of a steel hilt and double-edged blade with a superficial axial groove up to the middle, bearing its hallmark beside two four-pointed stars, probably Nasrid but of unknown origin. The hilt, made of brass, is formed by a spherical pommel with obverse and reverse circles, with a button at the end; a hilt that widens in the middle; a hollow quillon (arms of cross guard) with a poly-lobed upper profile and arms finished in the shape of a hook with fretwork circles on the outside. The niello decoration consists of intertwined circular bands that are superimposed on other longitudinal and traversal bands with inscriptions alluding to God. The intermediate spaces are filled with plant arabesques on the hilt and palmettes on the quillon. Small oblique damascene lines in gold make up the background of the whole piece. The scabbard, lost at an unknown time, would have had the same decoration, judging by the unfinished circles on the arms of the quillon.  
Surviving Andalusian armaments are rare and a set of Nasrid swords known as *jinetas* is particularly noteworthy. Their importance lies as much in the originality of their hilts, without equal in the period, as in the fact of being a genuine Nasrid production of luxury arms. This piece, while still a sumptuary object, belongs to a variety whose decoration, based in brass and niello, lacks the richness that characterises other *jineta* swords made of ivory or enamel.
ed60638d-d98c-52c9-b631-d363eb97fb51.short_description: Swords with horseshoe-shaped quillons were known as *jineta* swords. The hilts were usually made of precious metals and richly decorated, accentuating their value as symbols of prestige. This piece, with its brass and niello hilt, was a luxury item but is not as rich as other *jineta* swords.
ed60638d-d98c-52c9-b631-d363eb97fb51.dimensions: Length 140 cm, width of blade 4 cm, length of quillon 10 cm.
ed60638d-d98c-52c9-b631-d363eb97fb51.method_for_datation: Several similar pieces are in existence. One of them, acquired in Granada in 1812 by the National Library in Paris, preserves the motto of the Nasrid dynasty: 'Only God is victorious'. The other examples, which can be found in various museums and institutions as well as in private collections, also date from the 9th / 15th century.
ed60638d-d98c-52c9-b631-d363eb97fb51.method_for_provenance: There are no details about how the sword was moved from Andalusia to León. Before it was donated to the National Archaeological Museum, the sword was held by the image of the patron saint of the church of San Marcelo. However, this type of sword was produced exclusively during the Nasrid reign in Granada.
ed60638d-d98c-52c9-b631-d363eb97fb51.obtention: The sword was donated to the National Archaeological Museum by the parish priest of the church of San Marcelo (León), as a result of the mediation of Rodrigo Amador de los Ríos, on 20 September 1869.

edf3df89-1b5b-56bb-bbe1-38af5be2d483.name: Dress sword of a Landammann
edf3df89-1b5b-56bb-bbe1-38af5be2d483.description: Swords became the favoured weapons of citizens during the age of the French Revolution. A sumptuously designed sword served as a mark of civic distinction. The Landammann (chief official) of Appenzell, Jacob Zellweger-Zuberbühler (1770-1821), acquired this impressive item in Paris. He and his brother were successful merchants based in Trogen in Appenzell Ausserrhoden. Together with his wife and the official delegation of the Swiss Confederation, Jacob travelled to Paris to attend Napoleon’s coronation as emperor in 1804. While there, he took the opportunity to purchase this dress sword from the renowned goldsmith and sword maker Antoine-Modeste Fournera who had its splendid gilt-brass hilt elaborately embossed and engraved. A stylish dragon rests atop the pommel cap; the finish of the scabbard is equally lavish. The blade was made by the Coulaux Brothers in the Alsatian town of Klingenthal between 1801 and 1804; its reverse is marked “Manufacture National de Klingenthal”. The Swiss National Museum acquired this dress sword in 2015 from a Swiss family related to the original owner, Jacob Zellweger-Zuberbühler.

The revolver is fitted with chequered grip plates that are fixed to the frame with a screw installed in a round steel insert. On the barrel from the right side of the revolver a crowned oval with the letter R in the middle was engraved. Under the oval a star with what might be a letter g is engraved. The same letter is repeated on the frame at the base of the barrel.

f30819fe-fb4c-5ec9-a552-17d8231b324a.name: Coat of armour.
f30819fe-fb4c-5ec9-a552-17d8231b324a.description:
A suit of armour made from iron mail that would cover the body from the head to the knees. It has solid metal plates that cover the neck and the stomach – the latter being much larger in size than the former – to provide additional protection. A number of these chain-mail suits survive, often bearing signs of wear and tear from use in battle. One example reveals evidence of injury received on the left sleeve, where the metal chain is torn through.  
The sword shows a curved-edged blade which was popular among Muslim fighters, while the Crusaders preferred straight swords. Decorative features on swords are usually found at the hilt near the handle.  
The protective plates of the amour are decorated with geometric designs, a Mamluk blazon, and Arabic writing executed in gold *thuluth* script. Most of the decoration has worn away and it is possible to read only some of the words. These include: “made for … the exalted … the great … the lord”. From these words it is possible to conclude that this suit belonged to a ruler, military commander, or other high-ranking official.
f30819fe-fb4c-5ec9-a552-17d8231b324a.short_description: Mamluk military suits of armour decorated with gilded emblems, such as this one, were worn in battle against the Crusaders.
f30819fe-fb4c-5ec9-a552-17d8231b324a.method_for_datation: The blazon and phrases mentioned on the abdominal plate of this suit of armour indicate that it is from the Mamluk period.
f30819fe-fb4c-5ec9-a552-17d8231b324a.method_for_provenance: Although this armour is decorated with a Mamluk blazon and was found in Damascus, its provenance is not clear. The Mamluk period saw an increased regional mobility of people and goods, especially military. It was likely produced in Cairo or Damascus, since these were two major regional centres at this time.

f30ef8ba-a67a-55f8-91cb-fa65f19de25e.name: Sword.
f30ef8ba-a67a-55f8-91cb-fa65f19de25e.description:
A sword composed of a steel blade and a hilt made of animal horn. The scabbard is of gilded silver. The blade has decorative cartouches with inscriptions inside them. On the upper part of the blade there is a prominent medallion, which bears the following text: 'The work of al-Hajj Sanqur', and below this medallion is another inscription of the first verse of the chapter 'Mariam' from the Qur'an: 'Kaf Ha Ya Ayn Sad'. This line is followed byanother cartouche bearing the text, 'Sultan Fatih Muhammad Khan'.Below this cartouche are written verses 1 and 2 from the Qur'anic chapter 'al-Ha Mim', and 'Ain Sin Qaf'*.* The inscriptions and decorations that appear on the blade are executed in gold inlay. The scabbard is ornamented with vegetal decoration carved in high relief. The owner of the sword was the Ottoman Sultan Muhammad II Al Fatih ('The Conquerer').  
The Arabs imported swords from Iran and India. Quality swords were produced in Khurasan (Persia, now Iran), Damascus in Syria and Toledo in Spain.
f30ef8ba-a67a-55f8-91cb-fa65f19de25e.short_description: Ottomans excelled in making swords and their decoration rivalled that of the Iranians. In addition to their military use, swords bearing the names of Ottoman sultans were worn on gala celebrations at the court. This sword bears the name of Sultan Mohammad II and the name of its maker.
f30ef8ba-a67a-55f8-91cb-fa65f19de25e.initial_owner: Ottoman Sultan Muhammad II Al-Fatih (‘The Conqueror’); known in Turkey as Fatih Sultan Mehmet or Mehmet II.
f30ef8ba-a67a-55f8-91cb-fa65f19de25e.method_for_datation: The sword is dated based on the fact that the names of Ottoman Sultan Muhammad II and the name of the craftsman are recorded on it. In addition to this, the styles of the inscriptions, as well as the technique of manufacture, closely resemble the techniques that are specific to the Ottoman period.
f30ef8ba-a67a-55f8-91cb-fa65f19de25e.obtention: The sword was donated to the museum by Prince Yusuf Kamal, one of the princes of the family of Muhammad Ali, who was a collector of antiques. He donated a large number of ceramic and wooden objects and textiles to the museum.

f6368799-2300-59bb-921c-1730621f5530.name: Burgonet (*shishak*)
f6368799-2300-59bb-921c-1730621f5530.short_description: This morion (open helmet) belonged to the later Grand Vizir Mehmet Sokolovitsch (AD 1505–79). He was one of the many Christian boys selected for Devşirme (converted to Islam and trained for leadership positions). The sumptuous Oriental helmet is decorated with framed inscriptions containing appeals to Allah and verses from the Qur΄an. Sokolovitsch rose quickly at the court of Sultan Süleiman (AD 1494–66), retaining his position as Grand Vizir under the latter's successors, Selim III (AD 1524–74) and Murad III (AD 1546–95).

f918b78f-57d9-5c0d-a75f-075ce7156c35.name: Dagger
f918b78f-57d9-5c0d-a75f-075ce7156c35.short_description: Silver knife with silver handle and niello decoration on the front; metal on the backside and four Turkish coins along the edge of the sheath; a name (‘Jomaah Ali’) is inscribed on the blade of the dagger. This object is functional and can be used in everyday activities, but at the same time it is a prestigious object that every Bedouin man must have. The most common types of daggers in Jordan are the Yemeni dagger, the Hijazi and other local types.

f986df26-3b71-5c3e-8d5b-1a8c60864ea5.name: Yemeni dagger
f986df26-3b71-5c3e-8d5b-1a8c60864ea5.short_description: A dagger with a double-edged blade, an oblong-head hilt and silver filigree work in geometric designs; it is carried on a woollen belt with leather strap-work, usually with six asymmetrical suspension rings. Yemeni and Hijazi daggers have different shapes and their diffusion on the territory of Jordan shows how population movements, trade and exchange were common in the area.
